result: 80 subjects performed a continuous random dot motion task with 288 trials presented over 16 blocks, where baseline pupil diameter was computed as the average over 100 ms preceding target onset.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C82-C83 describe the experimental design, sample size, and methodological approach. These are straightforward methodological statements that are internally consistent and adequately described for replication.

result: Baseline pupil diameter (tonic arousal) displayed a non-monotonic relationship with both RT and RTcv, with slower RT on trials with higher baseline arousal levels.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C76 report statistically significant relationships (p=0.003 for RT, p=0.035 for RTcv) with appropriate statistical tests. The non-monotonic relationship is supported by chi-square tests and the direction of effect is clearly stated.

result: Pupil diameter response (phasic arousal) displayed a non-monotonic relationship with RT and an inverse linear relationship with RTcv, with best performance on trials with the largest pupil responses.
evaluation: Claims C7-C9 report highly significant statistical relationships (p<0.001 for both RT and RTcv) with appropriate chi-square tests. The findings are supported by Figure 1C and are internally consistent.

result: Phasic arousal (pupil response) was associated with faster CPP onset latency, steeper build-up rate (but not amplitude), and greater consistency (ITPC) of the CPP signal.
evaluation: Claims C11-C15 report statistically significant relationships for onset (p=0.018), build-up rate (p=0.035), and ITPC (p<0.001), with appropriate non-significant result for amplitude (p=0.15). The pattern is internally consistent and supported by Figure 2.

result: Pre-target α-band power showed an approximately linear relationship with RT (but not RTcv) and was inversely related to pupil diameter response, suggesting pre-target attentional engagement is related to phasic arousal.
evaluation: Claims C18-C21 report significant relationship with RT (p<0.001), non-significant with RTcv (p=0.48), and inverse relationship with pupil response (p<0.001). The inference about attentional engagement (C21) is reasonable given the established literature on α-band power.

result: Neither LHB amplitude nor slope varied with phasic arousal, suggesting phasic arousal does not influence the build-up rate of choice-related activity over motor cortex.
evaluation: Claims C23-C24 report non-significant relationships (p=0.63 for amplitude, p=0.20 for slope). The inference in C24 is appropriately cautious given the null results, though absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

result: The pupil response was not predictive of N2c or N2i latency, amplitude, or ITPC.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30 consistently report non-significant relationships across all N2 measures (all p>0.10). These null results are clearly stated with appropriate p-values and are important for understanding which processing stages are not affected by phasic arousal.

result: Hierarchical regression analysis revealed that pre-target α-power and CPP ITPC were the strongest predictors of RT variability due to phasic arousal, while CPP ITPC was the only predictor for RTcv, explaining 15.8% of RT variability.
evaluation: Claims C31-C38, C40-C41 describe a comprehensive hierarchical regression analysis with appropriate model selection procedures. Statistical tests are significant (p<0.001 for key predictors), and the stepwise elimination of CPP onset and build-up rate is justified. The marginal r² of 15.8% is modest but reasonable for neural predictors of behavior.

result: Baseline pupil diameter (tonic arousal) was not predictive of CPP onset or build-up rate but displayed an inverse relationship with CPP amplitude and consistency, indicating that higher arousal states are characterized by more variability in decision processing, which affects behavioral performance.
evaluation: Claims C42-C48 report appropriate statistical tests with significant inverse relationships for amplitude (p=0.01) and ITPC (p=0.002), and non-significant results for onset and build-up rate. The inference connecting higher arousal to more variability (C47-C48) is supported by the data and cited literature (Murphy et al., 2014b).

result: Pre-target alpha power varied with baseline pupil diameter in a non-monotonic manner, and there was an inverse relationship with LHB build-up rate but not amplitude.
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 report significant non-monotonic relationship for α-power (p=0.034), significant inverse relationship for LHB build-up rate (p<0.001), and non-significant for LHB amplitude (p=0.34). Results are supported by Figure 5 and appropriate statistical tests.

result: Baseline pupil diameter displayed a monotonic relationship with N2c amplitude (but not latency), with larger baseline pupil diameter associated with smaller N2c amplitudes, suggesting higher arousal has a negative impact on sensory encoding.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 report significant relationship with N2c amplitude (p<0.001) and non-significant with latency (p=0.75). The inference about negative impact on sensory encoding (C55) is reasonable but could benefit from additional mechanistic evidence.

result: N2c ITPC, N2i ITPC, N2i latency, and N2i amplitude did not vary with baseline pupil diameter.
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 consistently report non-significant relationships (all p>0.05). These null results are clearly stated and important for characterizing which aspects of target selection are not affected by tonic arousal.

result: For tonic arousal, N2c amplitude and CPP ITPC were the only parameters predictive of RT after model selection, while CPP ITPC was the only predictor for RTcv, indicating that CPP consistency explains unique variability in task performance associated with baseline pupil diameter changes.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 describe hierarchical regression with appropriate model selection (forward/backward algorithm). The results are internally consistent with the phasic arousal analysis and supported by Table 1. The conclusion about CPP consistency is well-supported.

result: Both tonic and phasic arousal were predictive of behavioral performance and distinct but overlapping sets of EEG signatures representing multiple information processing stages, with behavioral variability mediated by effects on attentional engagement, sensory processing, and decision processing variability.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C77-C78 provide a comprehensive summary of the main findings. These are well-supported by the individual analyses reported throughout the results section and represent appropriate integration of the findings.

result: The linear up-ramp model provided the best fit to the pupil data, and slow fluctuations in baseline pupil diameter (<0.01 Hz) drive the effect on task performance.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by model comparison (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and filtering analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 6). The inference about slow fluctuations (C85) is appropriately cautious and supported by the comparison of low-pass vs. band-pass filtered data.

result: There is no fixed delay between target selection and response, and there is variability in the duration of the sustained period of the task.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are inferences drawn from comparison of stimulus-locked and response-locked N2c signals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The logic is sound: if there were a fixed delay, the N2c amplitude would be similar in both alignments.

Claim C75 reports task performance with appropriate citation (Newman et al., 2017). This justifies the focus on RT measures rather than accuracy and is consistent with the experimental design using suprathreshold stimuli.

result: A negative correlation exists between baseline pupil diameter and pupillary response, and both tonic and phasic activity in neuromodulatory centers can affect behavior during decision-making through effects on attentional engagement, sensory processing, and decision formation across multiple timescales.
evaluation: Claims C106-C108 provide summary conclusions supported by the overall pattern of results and cited literature. The negative correlation (C106) is an established finding replicated here. The mechanistic conclusions (C107-C108) are appropriately cautious inferences from the data.

result: The manuscript cites extensive prior literature establishing that pupil diameter correlates with arousal and neuromodulatory activity, that CPP reflects evidence accumulation, that α-band power relates to attention, and that arousal affects neural variability and behavioral performance.
evaluation: Claims C10, C16-C17, C22, C67-C105 are all citation-based claims establishing the theoretical and empirical foundation for the study. These are appropriately cited and represent accurate characterizations of prior work. The authors build appropriately on established findings.
